ol96b1-bb5646.summary: Auriol's question whether God can give a wayfarer a light by which the truths of faith are known scientifically, occasioned by Lombard's profession of trust in divine help. It is famous for its theory of intuitive cognition. Opening arguments press for a middle light between faith and glory (Henry) and for Scotus's abstractive cognition of the deity; contrary arguments (Godfrey and others) deny both. (1) Henry's light is analyzed. A light clarifying terms and resolving objections is possible: it is the theological habit. A light showing the articles' connection under proper concepts is just abstractive cognition. A light showing the connection under the wayfarer's common concepts is impossible, because an inherence is seen only through its foundation, the proper concept of deity, and principles are known formally through their terms. Godfrey's denial is right in conclusion but wrong in reasons. (2) Scotus's view (abstractive cognition of the bare deity, not beatific, so possible for wayfarers and yielding a priori science of the necessary articles) is defended against Hervaeus by showing that abstraction can concern existence (astronomer, memory, imagination, signs). (3) Scotus errs in two ways. Against him Auriol argues, from experience (afterimages, dreams, fear, illusions, weak eyes) and a priori (God can preserve an absolute quality without the term of its relation; real dependence requires real distinction), that intuitive cognition can exist without the object's presence or existence. He then redefines intuitive cognition as a direct, presential, actualizing, existence-positing appearance, and abstractive cognition as a quasi-imaginative appearance in an absent mode, differing in mode not object, and rejects Gerard's definition. (4) Four conclusions: both modes are possible in the intellect (intuition is nobler, non-spatially presential, naturally caused and conserved by the object); both are possible regarding God; only intuitive cognition of God is beatific; and a quasi-imaginative cognition of the deity, if called a light, can be given to a wayfarer and would yield propter quid science of the articles. The replies apply these results throughout.
claims: No light can show the articles' truth under the common concepts a wayfarer has.
Knowledge of principles depends formally on proper concepts of their terms.
Abstractive (quasi-imaginative) cognition can concern a thing's existence and actuality.
Intuitive cognition can occur without the presence or existence of its object, naturally in sense and a fortiori by divine power.
Intuitive and imaginative cognition differ in mode of appearance, not object.
Intuitive cognition is a direct, presential, actualizing, existence-positing appearance.
Only intuitive cognition of the divine essence is beatific.
God could give a wayfarer quasi-imaginative cognition of the deity, yielding scientific knowledge of the articles.
The understanding the saints claim beyond faith is the theological habit.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e107.summary: Title of the question: whether God can give a wayfarer a light by whose power Catholic truths are known scientifically.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e116.summary: Connects the question to Lombard's prologue, where the Master professes trust in divine help, and opens the arguments that God can give a light strengthening the intellect so that the articles are clearly understood and conclusions drawn from them are scientifically known. First, every passive potency has a corresponding active potency, so every passive knowability in propositions can have an actualizing light. Propositions about the articles are either immediate, hence knowable, or mediate, and since there are no infinite middles they resolve into immediate ones. Second, God can make an intermediate between species maximally distant, so between the light of glory and the enigmatic light of faith he can make an intermediate light in which the articles are known scientifically.
claims: (Argument) Every passive knowability can be matched by an active light.
(Argument) Propositions about the articles resolve into immediate, self-knowable propositions.
(Argument) God can create a light between faith and glory.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e191.summary: Argues from three modes of knowing the same thing. An eclipse can be known by faith (hearing an astronomer), by science (calculation), and by intuition (seeing it), each with its own light. Believed truths have the lowest light (faith's enigma) and the highest (the clarity of heaven), so a middle, scientific light is possible.
claims: (Argument) Whatever can be known by faith and by intuition can also be known by science in a middle light.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e233.summary: Argues from Richard of St Victor, who holds that for the necessary truths of faith there are not only probable but necessary reasons, though they may escape our effort. Where necessary reasons exist, God can give a light in which these truths are scientifically known.
claims: (Argument) There are necessary reasons for the necessary truths of faith (Richard of St Victor).

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e264.summary: Argues that in God whatever is possible is necessary (Avicenna's necessary being), so knowing a divine truth to be possible is knowing it necessary. God can give a light showing the possibility of believed truths, because any syllogism proving their impossibility errs in matter (detectable by the special sciences) or in form (detectable by perfect logic), and God can give these sciences completely.
claims: (Argument) In divine matters the possible and the necessary coincide.
(Argument) Every argument against the articles errs in matter or form and can be refuted.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e303.summary: Argues that what God can give briefly and in passing (as he gave the prophets a light higher than faith) he can give lastingly, so he can give believers such a light permanently.
claims: (Argument) What God gives transiently he can give permanently.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e316.summary: Argues that knowledge of a conclusion is an effect of the premises, and God can produce any effect of a secondary cause without that cause. So he can give clear knowledge of believed truths without the premises, in a light higher than faith.
claims: (Argument) God can produce any effect of secondary causes directly.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e336.summary: Argues that knowledge of terms is really distinct from knowledge of their connection, so God could clarify the connection without clarifying the terms. He could give clear knowledge that God is three and one while the terms remain obscure, a light above faith and below beatific vision. Confirmed: God can give certain knowledge that Antichrist will come without clear knowledge of Antichrist's person.
claims: (Argument) Knowledge of terms and of their connection are really distinct.
(Argument) The connection could be clarified while the terms remain obscure.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e376.summary: Argues from authority. It is not safe to say the saints spoke falsely or boastfully of themselves. Augustine claims to reach certain science through the Catholic faith, Richard aims to bring necessary reasons for what we believe, and Augustine often distinguishes the light of the wise faithful from that of simple faith. So such a light must be posited.
claims: (Argument) The saints claim a knowledge of the articles beyond simple faith.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e409.summary: Rubric introducing arguments for Scotus's 'abstractive knowledge' of God.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e414.summary: First argument that God can give a wayfarer a clear, distinct abstractive knowledge of the deity's quidditative character, from which truths about persons and attributes could be concluded scientifically. Wherever memory of an intuited object remains, abstractive knowledge is possible, since memory abstracts from presence. Paul, rapt to the third heaven, saw the deity (Augustine) and retained its memory while still a wayfarer, so God could give such knowledge to any believer.
claims: (Argument) Memory of an intuited object is abstractive knowledge.
(Argument) Paul retained abstractive knowledge of the deity after his rapture.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e466.summary: Argues that whatever kind of cognition knows an act and its relation to an object can know the object. The act by which God is known and its relation to God are creatures and can be known abstractively, so God's essence can be known abstractively too.
claims: (Argument) What knows an act and its relation can know its object in the same way.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e484.summary: Argues that intuitive and abstractive knowledge differ only on the knower's side, not the object's. Even a thing's existence can be known abstractively (we can imagine how a rose exists on the branch). Different modes of knowing God involve no variety in God, so both are possible regarding God.
claims: (Argument) Intuitive and abstractive knowledge differ only in mode, not object.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e519.summary: Argues that whatever has essence conceptually distinct from existence can be conceived abstractively. In God essence and existence differ conceptually though not really, so God can be conceived abstractively. Confirmed: the essence can be conceived without truth, goodness or other attributes, so likewise without existence.
claims: (Argument) In God essence and existence differ conceptually.
(Argument) The divine essence can be conceived without its attributes.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e542.summary: Argues that abstractive knowledge abstracts from presence, and the deity can be conceived without its presence to us, which is only a relation of reason. So the deity can be conceived abstractively.
claims: (Argument) God's presence to us is a relation of reason.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e562.summary: States the premise of the next argument: creatures do not seem knowable by us in more ways than God.
claims: (Argument) God is not knowable in fewer ways than creatures.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e575.summary: Completes the argument: each thing is knowable insofar as it is in act, and what is more actual is more knowable and in more ways. A rose or any creaturely quiddity can be known both intuitively and abstractively, so the deity can be too.
claims: (Argument) Knowability follows actuality.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e591.summary: Argues that the intellect can separate what is prior from what is posterior. The deity, an 'ocean of infinite substance' (Damascene), is prior to existence, presence and every attribute, so it can be conceived without existence and presence, that is, abstractively.
claims: (Argument) The deity is prior to existence, presence and attributes.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e607.summary: Rubric and opening argument for the contrary (with Godfrey, against Henry's light). No light raising the intellect to scientific knowledge of the articles is possible, for if it were it would have been given to the Virgin, the apostles, the doctors or the masters. It was not: Mary walked by faith, which alone remained in her on Holy Saturday; Paul walked by faith; Augustine would have passed on such science; and no master, however excellent, claims at death to have science of the articles rather than belief.
claims: (Argument) No one, not even the Virgin or apostles, has received a scientific light of the articles.
(Argument) Faith alone remained in Mary on Holy Saturday.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e657.summary: Argues that if such a light were possible it would be infused at baptism, since grace in regeneration should give what is needed for spiritual perfection, as nature gives what is needed for natural perfection. No one experiences it, and the noblest habits cannot go unnoticed, so it is impossible.
claims: (Argument) A light needed for spiritual perfection would be given in baptism.
(Argument) The noblest habits cannot be hidden from their possessor.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e689.summary: Argues that such a light is incompatible with faith, the wayfarer's habit. It would remove faith's merit; it would contradict faith's obscurity, since faith concerns things not apparent (Heb 11:1) while the light would make them evident; faith and opinion are incompatible; and science cannot coexist with faith, or a mathematician could believe what he knows. (The sentence finishes in the next paragraph.)
claims: (Argument) Faith requires obscurity and merit, which a clarifying light would remove.
(Argument) Science and faith of the same object cannot coexist.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e720.summary: After the end of the previous argument (text displaced in the print), argues by dilemma: an intermediate light between faith and glory would be intermediate either by participation, and so nobler than both, as a mixture contains its components (as man is nobler than the elements), or by negation, and so separable from faith and able to be infused into an unbeliever. Neither is possible.
claims: (Argument) An intermediate light would be either nobler than glory or separable from faith.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e749.summary: Argues that evident knowledge of a principle requires distinct knowledge of its terms. Only the light of glory gives distinct knowledge of 'God' and 'Trinity of persons', and beatitude consists in exactly that, so no such intermediate light is possible.
claims: (Argument) Evident knowledge of a principle requires distinct knowledge of its terms.
(Argument) Distinct knowledge of God and the Trinity is beatitude.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e771.summary: Argues that two habits cannot principally adhere to the same truth, and the believer always holds the articles by faith, so he cannot be given another light by which he principally holds them.
claims: (Argument) Two habits cannot principally adhere to the same truth.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e784.summary: Rubric introducing certain thinkers' arguments against Scotus's abstractive knowledge.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e789.summary: First argument against abstractive knowledge of the deity in a wayfarer: all knowledge of the divine essence that is clear and distinct is beatific, and such abstractive knowledge would be, so it is impossible in this life.
claims: (Argument) Clear and distinct knowledge of the divine essence is beatific.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e808.summary: Argues that abstractive knowledge is not less perfect than intuitive, or God's knowledge of non-existent creatures (abstractive) would be less perfect than of existing ones (intuitive), and creaturely existence would perfect divine knowledge. So it is more or equally perfect, hence at least as beatific, and impossible for a wayfarer.
claims: (Argument) Abstractive knowledge is not less perfect than intuitive.
(Argument) Creaturely existence cannot perfect divine knowledge.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e837.summary: Argues that cognitions of the same object under the same formality are alike in being beatific or not. Intuitive and the proposed abstractive cognition both concern God under the formality of deity, so the abstractive would be beatific too. Confirmed: beatitude lies in knowing God clearly and nakedly through his essence, whether abstractively or intuitively.
claims: (Argument) Beatitude consists in clear knowledge of the divine essence, in either mode.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e861.summary: Argues that a relation of reason added to a cognition cannot make it beatific, since we are made blessed by the highest essence, not a relation of reason. Intuitive knowledge adds to abstractive only presence, a relation of reason. So if intuition is beatific, abstraction is too, and it is impossible in this life.
claims: (Argument) Intuitive cognition adds only presence, a relation of reason, to abstractive cognition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e887.summary: Two arguments. What includes existence in its quidditative concept cannot be conceived abstractively, since abstraction prescinds from existence and non-existence, and God, as necessary being, includes existence. And abstractive cognition presupposes intuitive (universals come from singulars intuited by sense), but the wayfarer cannot intuit God, so he cannot know God abstractively.
claims: (Argument) God's quidditative concept includes existence.
(Argument) Abstractive cognition presupposes intuitive cognition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e920.summary: Argues that the wayfarer knows abstractively only by abstracting from phantasms, and there is no phantasm of God, so God cannot be known abstractively in this life.
claims: (Argument) Wayfarer cognition abstracts from phantasms.
(Argument) There is no phantasm of God.
concepts: knowledge of God in this life

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e929.summary: Argues by dilemma that abstractive knowledge of God would bear either on a representation of God, and then God would not be known in himself and no representation suffices, or on the bare essence as it is, and then it would be intuitive.
claims: (Argument) No representation adequately represents the deity.
(Argument) Knowledge bearing on the bare essence is intuitive.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e954.summary: Argues that 'intuitive knowledge' in the intellect is improper, since concern with presence is a material condition of sensation, and 'abstractive knowledge' is a fictitious term. So the deity is not known in these ways.
claims: (Argument) Intuitive cognition properly belongs to sense, not intellect.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e974.summary: Rubric marking the beginning of the response to the question.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e979.summary: Lays out the response in four steps: the opposed opinions of two doctors (Henry and Godfrey), a modern view (Scotus's abstractive knowledge) examined for its truth, preliminaries for seeing the crux, and Auriol's own answer.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e999.summary: Rubric naming the first article: Henry of Ghent's opinion (Quodlibet XII q. 2; Summa q. 2 a. 1).

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1006.summary: States Henry's opinion: God can give a light by which the articles are known more clearly in this life than by faith, so that theologians know truths about God scientifically. Besides the nine initial arguments, it rests on the saints' authority. Augustine on John 1 distinguishes the 'mountains', lit by wisdom, from the 'hills', lit by faith; the lesser would not receive faith unless the greater had been enlightened by Wisdom. And in the letter to Severinus he says the unity and distinction in God must be believed on authority, and its understanding is reached only with God's help.
claims: (Reported) God can give a light by which theologians know the articles scientifically.
(Reported) Augustine distinguishes a light of wisdom for the greater from faith for the lesser.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1078.summary: Analyzes Henry's light into three possible senses. (a) A light clarifying the terms of the articles and removing apparent contradictions and defects of reasons, without seeing the connection of terms: God can give this in the highest degree, and study already gives some of it (as in the previous question). (b) A light by which the connection of terms is seen under proper and distinct concepts of the deity and Trinity: possible, but identical with Scotus's abstractive knowledge, which Henry did not intend. (c) A light by which the connection is seen under the common, non-proper concepts wayfarers have: impossible. An inherence, being a relation, can be seen only if its foundation and the ground of founding are seen, and only the proper concept of the deity grounds 'God is three and one'. Any other concept is of another being or is a common concept such as 'first being', which does not ground the Trinity, since the Trinity belongs to God by the proper character of deity.
claims: God can give a light that clarifies terms and resolves objections, and theological study partially acquires it.
A light seeing the articles' connection through proper concepts of the deity is possible but is abstractive knowledge.
No light can show the articles' connection under the common concepts wayfarers have.
Seeing a relation requires knowing its foundation and ground.
The Trinity belongs to God through the proper character of deity, not through any common concept.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1212.summary: Further proof against Henry's light in sense (c). An inherence would be seen from the terms, from prior propositions, or immediately. Not from the terms as wayfarers conceive them, which do not cause it. Not from prior propositions: neither by descent from a universal, since the Trinity belongs to God by a proper character, nor by likeness, since dissimilarity to the Trinity exceeds similarity (Augustine) and argument from likeness is valid only if a common reason grounds the predicate in both (as with the immortality of two souls). Not immediately, since a thing is known only as it is apt to be known and the inherence is a caused, secondary truth. Against the Antichrist example: knowing that Antichrist will come without knowing his figure is believing, not clearly knowing; one can adhere by faith to a connection of unclear terms.
claims: The inherence in the articles cannot be seen from wayfarer concepts, from prior propositions, or immediately.
Argument from likeness is valid only where a common reason grounds the predicate.
Dissimilarity of any creature to the Trinity exceeds similarity.
Knowing a connection without clear terms is belief, not clear knowledge.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1314.summary: Further proof against Henry's light. God cannot separate from an act the formal character under which it reaches its object, as seeing a wall through its color cannot be separated from apprehending the color, nor choosing means from intending the end. The formal character by which the intellect grasps the connection of terms in immediate propositions is the proper concept of each term (we know principles insofar as we know their terms). So no light can show the connection of a proposition without proper concepts of its terms.
claims: God cannot separate an act from the formal character under which it reaches its object.
Proper concepts of the terms are the formal reason by which a principle is known.
No light can reveal a proposition's connection without proper concepts of its terms.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1358.summary: Rejects the reply that knowledge of terms efficiently causes knowledge of the principle, as premises cause knowledge of the conclusion. That holds for separate knowledge of the terms, but within knowledge of the principle the terms function formally, not efficiently, as the principle does in knowing a conclusion and the end does in desiring means.
claims: Within knowledge of a principle, knowledge of the terms functions formally, not efficiently.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1389.summary: Further proof: to know an inherence scientifically as necessary is to know it from the terms, since no relation is necessary of itself and its necessity comes from elsewhere. So an inherence cannot be known scientifically unless the terms are conceived under the character that grounds it.
claims: No relation is necessary of itself.
Scientific knowledge of an inherence requires conceiving the terms under the character that grounds it.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1409.summary: Further proof by analogy. As spoken terms are parts of a spoken proposition, term-concepts are parts of the concept of a principle, and they must be proper, not confused or common, concepts. A proposition immediate under a proper concept is not immediate under a common one: 'a triangle has three angles equal to two right angles' is immediate, but 'a figure has three...' is not and can be proved from the lower. So a proposition's connection cannot be clearly and nakedly known without proper concepts of its terms.
claims: Concepts of terms are parts of the concept of a principle.
Immediacy holds under proper concepts but not under common ones.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1453.summary: Final proof and conclusion of the first article. As an inherence relates to its proper terms in being, so in knowing, and it cannot exist without them. So no light can show or clearly know the inherence of the articles. A light can be given that clarifies the terms, removes apparent conflicts arising from opposing reasons, and supports the connection in the minds of the weak who might fall away without probable reasons. That light is the theological habit described before, and all Augustine's texts refer to it, not to Henry's impossible, fictitious light.
claims: No light can make the inherence of the articles clearly known in this life.
God can give a light that clarifies terms and removes objections, and it is the theological habit.
Augustine's authorities refer to the theological habit, not to a scientific light.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1493.summary: Rubric naming Godfrey of Fontaines' opinion (Quodlibet III q. 10; IV q. 19).

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1500.summary: States Godfrey's opposite view: such a light is impossible, chiefly because it could not coexist with faith, supported by the six arguments of the third group. Auriol grants the conclusion as true (for the light Henry intends) but says the arguments do not hold, as the replies will show. Whether such a light is incompatible with faith needs examination but belongs to book 3 of the Sentences, so he sets it aside.
claims: (Reported) A scientific light is impossible because it cannot coexist with faith.
Godfrey's conclusion is true, but his arguments fail.
Whether such a light is compatible with faith belongs to book 3.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1529.summary: Rubric, badly corrupted in the transcription, introducing Scotus's opinion (second article).

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1542.summary: Introduces, in a partly corrupt text, the modern view (Scotus) that comes closer to the truth: God can give a light in which the articles are known under proper concepts, God under the proper and distinct character of deity. That light is just abstractive knowledge of the bare divine essence, and its proponents argue for it in four steps.
claims: (Reported) God can give abstractive knowledge of the bare divine essence under its proper character.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1564.summary: First step of Scotus's view: defining the two cognitions. Intuitive cognition concerns the presence and existence of a thing and terminates at it as existing in itself. Abstractive cognition abstracts from being and non-being, existence and presence. I intuit a rose when I see it present and know it abstractively when I consider its nature. Both are possible in the intellect: an angel intuits a rose while it exists and considers its essence abstractively even when it does not.
claims: (Reported) Intuitive cognition terminates at the thing as present and existing.
(Reported) Abstractive cognition abstracts from existence and presence.
(Reported) Both kinds occur in intellect, as in angels.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1595.summary: Second step of Scotus's view: God can do by will alone whatever he does through his essence. Through his essence he moves the blessed intellect to clear, naked, intuitive knowledge of it, as present and existing. So by will alone he can move the intellect to clear knowledge of the essence. Since that knowledge terminates at the essence under the character by which the intellect is moved, which is the command of the will and not the essence's presence and existence, it abstracts from existence and is abstractive.
claims: (Reported) God can do by will alone what he does through his essence.
(Reported) Knowledge caused by divine will alone would be abstractive.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1640.summary: Third step of Scotus's view: such knowledge is possible for a wayfarer. Any knowledge that does not make him blessed is possible, and abstractive knowledge of the divine essence is not beatific, only intuitive knowledge is. Seeing God through his essence, which is beatific, is intuitive, and abstractive knowledge could exist even if, per impossibile, God did not exist, as a rose's quiddity is known when no rose exists.
claims: (Reported) Only intuitive knowledge of God is beatific.
(Reported) Abstractive knowledge of the divine essence is possible for wayfarers.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1669.summary: Fourth step of Scotus's view: from such knowledge theological truths could be known scientifically and a priori. Whoever knows a subject under its proper quidditative character can know all truths virtually contained in it, since principles predicate proper attributes of the subject's definition (Grosseteste, second mode of per se). Science abstracts from the subject's existence, which is why there is no science of singulars. So a wayfarer with abstractive knowledge of the deity could know scientifically the articles that are necessary by nature, not those that are voluntarily contingent. Auriol calls the view very reasonable, beautiful and subtle.
claims: (Reported) Knowing a subject's quiddity virtually contains all truths of its science.
(Reported) Science abstracts from the existence of its subject.
(Reported) Abstractive knowledge of the deity would yield scientific knowledge of the necessary articles.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1734.summary: Rubric introducing Hervaeus Natalis's attack on Scotus (Quodlibet II q. 5).

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1741.summary: Hervaeus's first objection to Scotus's conclusion. Every first cognition, preceded by no other, terminates at the thing in its entity and is therefore intuitive, since it grasps the thing under its fundamental reality rather than secondary aspects. Knowledge of the divine quiddity is first: it cannot come through a creature in which the deity shines (impossible objectively), nor through prior knowledge of God's existence (existence would then precede essence). So knowledge of the divine quiddity is always intuitive.
claims: (Reported) Every first cognition of a thing is intuitive.
(Reported) Knowledge of the divine quiddity is necessarily first and so intuitive.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1796.summary: Hervaeus's second objection. Abstractive knowledge of God's quiddity would be of the 'what the name means' or the 'what the thing is'. The former gives no more than we have of fictions. The latter requires knowing the nature as actually existing or able to exist, and God's essence, known perfectly, is known as actually existing, not merely possible. So such knowledge is always intuitive.
claims: (Reported) Real quidditative knowledge of God must know him as actually existing.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1829.summary: Hervaeus's third objection: knowing what something is presupposes knowing whether it is (actually in God's case), so abstractive knowledge of God's quiddity would bear on his existence and be intuitive. Then three objections to Scotus's proof. It falsely assumes God impresses the vision on the blessed by natural necessity, whereas God acts freely in creatures. If the assumption were true, the principle that God can do by will alone what he does through his essence would fail, since what belongs to God by natural necessity does not fall under his will (the Father's generating the Son is not subject to his will). (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: (Reported) Knowing what a thing is presupposes knowing that it is.
(Reported) God acts freely, not by natural necessity, in creatures.
(Reported) What is in God by natural necessity is not subject to his will.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1889.summary: Hervaeus's third objection to Scotus's proof: by the same reasoning God could produce intuitive knowledge without the object's presence, since he could produce by will alone what the essence's motion produces, which Scotus's followers deny.
claims: (Reported) Scotus's principle would allow intuitive cognition without a present object.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1909.summary: Rubric introducing a defense of Scotus against Hervaeus, proving that abstractive cognition can concern a thing's actuality.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1916.summary: Begins Auriol's defense of Scotus: the position stands unless more is brought. Hervaeus's first three arguments rest on the false supposition that a thing's actual existence cannot be known abstractively.
claims: A thing's actuality and existence can be known abstractively.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1934.summary: First proof that existence can be known abstractively. Astronomical knowledge is scientific and hence abstractive, yet it concerns actual existence: future (an eclipse will occur at this hour), past (it occurred), and present (someone shut in a room can say the eclipse is now beginning or ending) without seeing it.
claims: Scientific, abstractive knowledge can concern a thing's actual existence in past, present or future.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1963.summary: Second proof: memory and remembering belong to abstractive knowledge, yet they reach a thing's existence and actuality, since we remember only what was actual. (The end of the text is corrupt.)
claims: Memory is abstractive yet concerns actual existence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1976.summary: Third proof: imagination is the abstractive cognition directly opposed to intuition, yet it bears directly on existence and presence. One in a room can imagine 'now there is an eclipse', and one who hears a voice without seeing can imagine 'this is such a man'.
claims: Imagination, though abstractive, bears on existence and presence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e1995.summary: Fourth proof: demonstrative 'quia' knowledge is scientific and so abstractive. The astronomer demonstrates that the earth is actually round and the heavens spherical, and the physician infallibly knows from urine that a disease is present. So abstractive knowledge can concern actuality, presence and existence.
claims: Demonstrative knowledge can establish actual existence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2015.summary: Applies this to Hervaeus's three arguments. Even if knowledge of God's quiddity reaches God's reality, it does so abstractively, quasi-imaginatively, as the astronomer in his room knows the eclipse is happening. Likewise abstractive knowledge can grasp God's 'what' and that he really exists, imaginatively. The third argument fails the same way.
claims: Knowledge of God's quiddity and existence can be abstractive, in an imaginative mode.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2050.summary: Answers Hervaeus's three objections to Scotus's proof, which rest on two false imaginings. Scotus did not say the essence moves the blessed intellect by natural necessity. It moves executively, at the command of the will that determines it, as human nature generates only by the will's determination. So the first objection only shows the motion is free, not that it is not executively from the essence, and the second would hold only if Scotus allowed natural necessity. The third assumes intuition is purely absolute, whereas for Scotus it includes an actual relation to the object's existence, so separating them is contradictory. Scotus deliberately said 'whatever' (absolute things), not relations: God cannot make a relative without its term (a Father without the Son), but abstractive cognition includes no such relation.
claims: For Scotus the divine essence moves the blessed intellect executively, at the will's command.
For Scotus intuitive cognition includes an actual relation to the object's existence.
God cannot produce a relation without its term, but abstractive cognition includes no such relation.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2159.summary: Rubric for the third article: preliminaries to solving the question, beginning with the first point on which Scotus's opinion fails.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2168.summary: Assesses Scotus's view. It is right on two points: there can be abstractive knowledge of the deity, and it is not beatific and so is possible for a wayfarer. Hence a light can be given in which theological truths are known scientifically. It errs on two points: that intuitive cognition cannot exist without the object's actual presence, and its definitions of intuitive and abstractive cognition. Auriol then gives the case for inseparability. A relative denomination cannot exist without its term (no Father without a Son), and 'I see Peter' implies 'Peter exists', so intuition cannot exist without the present thing; moreover the actual relation to the object is really identical with intuition, though formally distinct.
claims: Abstractive knowledge of the deity is possible and not beatific.
God can give a light by which theological truths are known scientifically.
Scotus errs in holding intuition inseparable from the object's presence.
Scotus's definitions of intuitive and abstractive cognition are inadequate.
(Argument) Intuition is a relative denomination requiring its term.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2240.summary: Second argument for inseparability. Intuition cannot exist without the difference distinguishing it from abstraction, or it would become abstraction. That difference is not in the object, since everything intuited can be known abstractively, but in requiring the object's existence. So intuition cannot be separated from the object's existence.
claims: (Argument) Intuition differs from abstraction by requiring the object's existence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2272.summary: Third argument for inseparability: as abstraction relates to the object in cognized being, intuition relates to the object in real being. Abstraction cannot exist without the object in cognized being, so intuition cannot exist without it in real being.
claims: (Argument) Intuition requires the object in real being.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2285.summary: Fourth argument: touch and taste require the object's presence no less than sight, and one cannot touch or taste what is absent, so neither can one see or intuit it.
claims: (Argument) All senses, including sight, require the object's presence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2296.summary: Fifth argument: what, once removed, makes us say there is no intuition is required for intuition. When the object is removed we say a person does not see but is deceived, as with the bewitched.
claims: (Argument) Without the object we speak of deception, not seeing.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2307.summary: Gives a final argument for inseparability (otherwise beatific intuition could exist without God's existence) and then Auriol's thesis: intuitive cognition can occur when the thing is absent and non-existent. He proves it first by experience, which is to be preferred to logical arguments since science and first principles arise from it, using five experiences of sensory intuition without a present object. (1) Afterimages after looking at the sun, which Augustine calls the remnants of the form in sense and a vision. (2) Dreams, where according to Averroes the imagination moves the common sense and the particular senses, so a person sees and feels without an external object. (3) The fearful and sick, who hear and see terrors. (4) The bewitched, who see castles, dogs and hares that are not there. (5) Weak eyes, for which a red afterimage colors everything. Since intellectual intuition is named after sensory intuition and the intellect is more independent than sense, a fortiori intellectual intuition can be separated from the object's presence.
claims: Intuitive cognition can occur without the object's presence or existence.
Experience is to be preferred to logical arguments.
Sensory intuitions such as afterimages, dreams and illusions occur without present objects.
A fortiori, intellectual intuition can occur without its object.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2479.summary: Adds an argument from divine power: God is more powerful than art or nature, and art (in illusions) and nature (in dreams, fear, illness) produce vision without a present object, so a fortiori God can. Two evasions are raised: such visions are false and deceptive, and they are only judgments of the common sense, not seeings. Answer to the first: it confirms the thesis, since any act in the power of sight shares the specific character of vision, and Augustine and Averroes call these acts visions in the eye and the five senses. So no vision by its specific character requires the object's presence.
claims: God can do a fortiori what art and nature do in producing vision without an object.
Every act in the visual power shares the specific character of vision.
No vision by its species requires the object's presence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2542.summary: Continues the answer to the first evasion: truth and falsity belong to numerically the same cognition with a change only in the thing (Categories: the same belief that Socrates sits becomes false when he stands). So false visions are the same in reality as true ones; the reality of a vision does not require the object, though its truth, a relation of conformity, does. Against the second evasion: Augustine and Averroes place such appearances in the particular sense; the common sense acts only when the particular senses act; its judgment requires an appearance in the eye, which is the vision; it judges nothing outside, while these appearances are judged outside; and even in the common sense it would be intuition without presence. Then the a priori proof: God can do whatever implies no contradiction and preserve the foundation of a relation when the term is destroyed, as Socrates survives his son. Intuition is something absolute grounding a relation to its object, so God can preserve it without the object. Against the claim that the relation is really identical with the absolute and only formally distinct: a really dependent thing and a really independent thing cannot be really the same, since real predicates require real distinction in their subject. Intuition in its absolute reality is independent (except efficiently), while its relation depends on its term.
claims: Truth and falsity can belong to the same cognition with change only in the object.
The reality of a vision does not require the object; its truth does.
God can preserve the foundation of a relation without its term.
Intuitive cognition is an absolute quality grounding a relation to the object.
A really dependent and a really independent thing cannot be really identical; formal distinction is insufficient.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2712.summary: Further a priori argument: God can preserve any thing without another on which it depends only efficiently, and the absolute reality of intuition is a quality depending on the object only efficiently. If it essentially required the object as term, it would not be a quality or absolute. Auriol then answers the arguments for inseparability. Intuition is not merely a relative denomination, and it relates only to the object as intuited. Requiring existence is not the difference between intuition and abstraction. Intuition requires the object in intuited being, not real being. Taste and touch also occur without objects in dreams. The bewitched are said not to see in the sense that their vision is false, as one who understands something false is said not to understand. Intuition of God cannot exist without God, but because God causes and conserves it, not because it requires God as object.
claims: God can preserve what depends on another only efficiently without that other.
Intuitive cognition requires the object only in intuited being, not real being.
Intuitive cognition of God requires God's existence as cause and conserver, not as object.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2823.summary: Rubric for the second point on which Scotus's opinion fails, where the true definitions of intuitive and abstractive cognition are given.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e2830.summary: Gives Auriol's own definitions. Scotus's definitions fail: abstraction can concern existence, and intuition does not require presence. Coining terms as Hilary allows, Auriol defines intuitive cognition as direct, presential cognition of its object, actualizing it and positing its existence. Imaginative cognition (the most abstractive) and ocular cognition (the most intuitive) differ not in object but in mode, by four conditions that ocular vision has and imagination lacks. (1) Directness: imagination reaches existence inferentially, from cause, effect or sign (the astronomer, the physician). (2) Presentiality: imagination reaches even present things in an absent mode, while sight reaches even absent things presentially. (3) Actuation: sight makes the object appear as actual. (4) Positing of existence: sight makes the non-existent appear existing. Transferred to the intellect, intuition is a presential, actualizing, direct appearance of a thing's existence, whether or not it exists; the other mode is better called 'imaginative' (Aristotle and Averroes speak of imagination through the intellect), since 'abstractive' suits the knowledge of universals. The difference lies in presentiality versus absence as modes of knowing, not as features of the object.
claims: Intuitive and abstractive cognition differ in mode, not object.
Intuitive cognition is direct, presential, actualizing and existence-positing.
Imaginative (abstractive) cognition lacks these four conditions even when it concerns present, existing things.
Cognition is a formal appearance in which things appear objectively.
'Imaginative' is a better name than 'abstractive' for non-intuitive intellectual cognition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3114.summary: Rubric announcing that the definition given by Gerard (of Bologna?) in his Quodlibet q. 9 is therefore inadequate.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3121.summary: Rejects the definition of intuition as cognition of a thing wholly immediate, without species, image or other object, terminating at its presence. First, dream-vision is by species, derived from imagination, and not terminated at a real presence, yet it is true intuition. Second, the definition fits imaginative cognition too, which also reaches its object without an objective medium: otherwise imagined Rome would be an idol of Rome, and the house in the builder's mind not the house outside, against Metaphysics VII. Imagination may use a species as a formal medium just as sight does. An immediate imagination without species would still not be intuition, since it reaches its object in an absent mode.
claims: Dream-vision is genuine intuition even though it uses species and lacks real presence.
Imaginative cognition also reaches its object without an objective medium.
Immediacy does not distinguish intuition from imagination; the presential mode does.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3195.summary: Rubric for the fourth article, which answers the question directly.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3203.summary: Announces that the direct answer will be given in four propositions.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3212.summary: First proposition: intuitive and imaginative cognition are both possible in the intellect. First objection: the intellect abstracts from here and now, while intuition seems material, being presential (simultaneity in duration) and actualizing.
claims: Intuitive and imaginative cognition are both possible in the intellect.
(Objection) Intuitive cognition is material and so unfit for the intellect.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3234.summary: Second objection: intellectual intuition would deceive, since immaterial cognition persists and would keep representing an absent thing as present without the intellect detecting it. Confirmed: on this view God would be deceived, intuiting future things as present. Auriol nonetheless proves the first proposition. Intuitive cognition is nobler than imaginative: more desirable (one who imagines wants to see), more delightful, clearer, more certain (sight is experiential; error belongs to phantasy), and so more perfect and uniting more fully with the object. The intellect, nobler than sense, must have the noblest mode of knowing, intuition, and it obviously has the imaginative mode.
claims: (Objection) Intellectual intuition would make the intellect err about absent objects.
Intuitive cognition is nobler than imaginative: more desirable, delightful, clear, certain and perfect.
The intellect must have the noblest mode of cognition, intuition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3325.summary: Further proof from 1 Corinthians 13: we see now 'in a mirror, in an enigma' (imaginatively) and then 'face to face' (intuitively), so both are in the intellect. Answer to the first objection: sensory vision is material because its directness, presence and actuality are spatial (a straight line from the eye, spatial opposition, here and now). In intellectual intuition these conditions are spiritual: presence without distance, inside or outside, here or there. Answer to the second: in the natural order intuition is impressed and conserved by the object, like light by the sun, and ceases when the object is absent, so it does not deceive; imaginative cognition persists at the will's command. God's intuition of the future is a presential appearance for the 'now' when the thing will exist, so it is true. In this life we do not notice intellectual intuition because it is joined to sensory intuition, as the geometer intuits a triangle in the dust with intellect and sense at once (Averroes).
claims: 1 Cor 13 attests both imaginative and intuitive intellectual cognition.
Intellectual intuition has spiritual, non-spatial presentiality.
Naturally, intuition is caused and conserved by its object and ceases in its absence.
God's intuition of future things is presential for the 'now' in which they will exist.
In this life intellectual intuition goes unnoticed because it accompanies sensory intuition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3468.summary: Rubric announcing that both kinds of cognition are possible regarding God.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3475.summary: Second proposition: the intellect can have both quasi-imaginative and quasi-intuitive cognition of God, as of anything else. Neither God's being pure subsisting being nor his real presence everywhere rules out imaginative cognition. Pure being can be conceived in an absent mode, and one can be certain imaginatively that something is present (even present by indwelling) without seeing it presentially.
claims: Both imaginative and intuitive cognition of God are possible.
Pure being and real omnipresence do not exclude imaginative cognition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3515.summary: Supports the second proposition: God's essence can appear to and conform the intellect in as many ways as a creature's quiddity, and a rose can appear both presentially and imaginatively.
claims: The divine essence can appear in as many modes as a creaturely quiddity.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3535.summary: Supports the second proposition: pure act can be known imaginatively, or metaphysics could not prove that God is pure act. The only reason given for knowing God solely intuitively is that he is known as pure, actually existing act, so there is no reason he cannot be known imaginatively. All grant the blessed know him intuitively, so both are possible. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: Metaphysics knows God as pure act imaginatively.
The blessed know God intuitively.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3564.summary: Rubric announcing that only intuitive cognition of God is beatific.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3573.summary: Third proposition: knowledge of the distinct, bare divine essence is beatific only if intuitive. Beatitude is the intellect's best operation (Ethics I, X), and imaginative cognition of God, however distinct, is not the best, since intuition is nobler (first proposition).
claims: Beatitude consists in the intellect's best operation.
Only intuitive cognition of the divine essence is beatific.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3602.summary: Supports the third proposition: what does not satisfy but excites desire is not the ultimate end. Imaginative cognition of God, like that of any beloved, excites desire to see, so it is not beatitude.
claims: Imaginative cognition of God excites desire to see and so is not the last end.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3620.summary: Supports the third proposition: no cognition that leaves the intellect in some darkness about God beatifies, and imaginative cognition, however distinct, leaves God absent until he is seen presentially.
claims: Imaginative cognition of God leaves some darkness, since God remains absent.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3643.summary: Rubric announcing that a light can be given to the wayfarer by which he can know the believed truths scientifically.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3650.summary: Fourth proposition: if quasi-imaginative cognition of the proper divine essence is called a light, it can be given to a wayfarer, and through it he would know the articles scientifically. It is not ruled out as beatific (just disproved), nor by a supposed necessary connection with intuition. Abstractive knowledge can be given of things never intuited (Solomon's infused wisdom, infused color species in one born blind, angels' infused species), and whatever their connection in generation, in being they are separable, so God can give one without the other. Such cognition gives scientific knowledge, since it leads to the cause and shows that the believed truths cannot be otherwise: the deity is the foundation of all that is believed of God. So a wayfarer could know the reason why, for some truths as possible (God could become incarnate) and for others as actual (God is three and one).
claims: Quasi-imaginative cognition of the divine essence can be given to a wayfarer.
Abstractive cognition can exist without prior intuition, by divine infusion.
Such cognition would give scientific, propter quid knowledge of the articles.
The deity is the foundation of all truths believed of God.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3772.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the objections.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3777.summary: Replies to the first argument: knowability lies in propositions through concepts, not words. Under the concepts wayfarers have, the articles are not knowable whatever light is given, unless the light supplies proper concepts, and that light is just quasi-imaginative cognition. The propositions are immediate under proper concepts but mediate under common ones, and the middle can be reached only by a light leading to proper concepts.
claims: Knowability belongs to propositions through concepts, not words.
The articles are immediate under proper concepts and mediate under common ones.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3819.summary: Replies to the second argument: God can make a middle light between glory and faith, namely quasi-imaginative cognition of the deity, but not the light sought, one that works while the concepts of the terms stay confused.
claims: The only possible middle light between faith and glory is imaginative cognition of the deity.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3835.summary: Replies to the third argument: the only middle scientific cognition between faith and vision is that imaginative cognition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3847.summary: Replies to the argument from Richard of St Victor: by 'necessary reasons' he means highly probable and effective reasons, not strictly necessary ones, and so does Anselm when he claims to give necessary reasons for the Incarnation.
claims: Richard's and Anselm's 'necessary reasons' are highly probable, not strictly necessary.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3865.summary: Replies to the fifth argument: God can give a light showing that the divine truths are not impossible on the basis of propositions taken from creatures, but not that they could not be impossible from the proper character of deity, without giving knowledge of that character. Refuting every faulty syllogism does not establish possibility, since a contradiction may come from the proper character of deity, which is unknown to us.
claims: Refuting objections does not prove the possibility of the articles.
The articles might conflict with the unknown proper character of deity.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3891.summary: Replies to the sixth argument: God gave the prophets not a light producing evidence but one producing stronger adherence than faith, through the syllogism discussed in the previous question.
claims: Prophetic light produced stronger adherence, not evidence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3909.summary: Replies to the seventh and eighth arguments. Knowledge of the premises taken separately efficiently causes knowledge of the conclusion, but that knowledge has the conclusion as object and the principle's truth as formal reason, one cognition reaching both. So God cannot separate it from the principle's truth. The same holds of principles and their terms.
claims: Knowledge of a conclusion is one cognition reaching both conclusion and principle.
God cannot separate knowledge of a conclusion from its principle.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3935.summary: Replies to the argument from the saints: the science and understanding of believed things they claim beyond faith is the theological habit described in the previous question.
claims: The saints' claimed understanding is the theological habit.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3948.summary: Replies to the second set of arguments (for Scotus's abstractive cognition): their conclusion is true. Those relying on the distinction of essence from existence and presence are weak, since they assume existence and presence cannot be known imaginatively.
claims: The conclusion that God can be known abstractively is true.
Arguments from separating essence and existence wrongly assume existence cannot be known imaginatively.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3971.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the first set of contrary arguments.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e3976.summary: Replies to the argument that no saint received such a light: the conclusion against Henry's light is true but the reasons fail. It is not proven the apostles and doctors lacked it: Paul's 'we walk by faith' speaks for the Church, and the doctors could not pass it on because we lack the light to follow their scientific procedure, as a dull student cannot follow geometry. Or it was possible but not expedient for them, since it would not have served merit.
claims: It is not proven that the apostles or doctors lacked such a light.
Paul's 'we walk by faith' is spoken in the person of the Church.
Such a light may have been possible but not expedient for merit.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4020.summary: Replies to the baptism argument: the light need not be given in baptism, since not all believers need it, only those who wish to acquire the science of theology, which cannot be had without it.
claims: A scientific light of theology would be needed only by students of theology, not all believers.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4033.summary: Replies to the incompatibility-with-faith argument. Such a light would still be possible in a wayfarer even if it excluded faith, since only intuition, not science, removes one from the state of the way. And whether faith can coexist with it is doubtful, to be treated elsewhere. (The text is partly corrupt.)
claims: Only intuitive vision, not science, takes one out of the state of the wayfarer.
Whether such a light is compatible with faith is left open.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4053.summary: Replies to the 'middle light' dilemma: the light is a middle by participation, approaching both extremes, not blended from them, and such a middle need not exceed the nobler extreme (the rational soul stands between intelligences and natural forms without exceeding the intelligences). Even blended middles do not always exceed the nobler extreme: a mule is not nobler than a horse, nor red than white (Metaphysics X).
claims: A middle by participation need not exceed the nobler extreme.
Blended middles do not always exceed the nobler extreme.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4088.summary: Replies to the argument about distinct knowledge of terms: rightly, no light gives evident knowledge of an article without distinct knowledge of its terms. But it is false that only the light of glory gives such knowledge of God, since distinct, quasi-imaginative, non-visual knowledge is possible below glory.
claims: Distinct knowledge of the terms is required for evidence of the articles.
Distinct, non-visual knowledge of God is possible below the light of glory.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4111.summary: Replies to the 'two habits' argument: someone with such a light could adhere both by faith, on Christ's authority, and by the light, since authority and reason can concur. Or, if he did not adhere by faith, he would not thereby leave the state of the way.
claims: Authority and reason can concur in adherence to the same truth.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4131.summary: Rubric introducing the replies to the last set of arguments.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4136.summary: Replies to the first argument against abstractive cognition of God: quasi-imaginative cognition of the deity, however distinct, is not beatific; only intuitive cognition is.
claims: Imaginative cognition of the deity is not beatific.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4154.summary: Replies to the second argument: in God intuitive cognition is nobler than imaginative, but it does not follow that creatures' actuality perfects divine knowledge, since God had intuitive cognition of non-existent things from eternity, as will be shown later.
claims: God has eternal intuitive cognition of non-existent things.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4170.summary: Replies to the third argument: intuitive and imaginative cognition share an object but do not reach it in the same way and differ in kind, so one being beatific does not make the other so.
claims: Intuitive and imaginative cognition of the same object differ in kind.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4186.summary: Replies to the fourth argument: what beatifies is not the relation of presence but the divine essence grasped in the noblest mode, the intuitive.
claims: Beatitude comes from the divine essence grasped intuitively, not from a relation of presence.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4198.summary: Replies to the fifth argument: the divine essence and existence do differ conceptually (to be shown later), and God's existence and actuality can in any case be known quasi-imaginatively.
claims: Divine essence and existence differ conceptually.
God's existence can be known imaginatively.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4211.summary: Replies to the sixth and seventh arguments: 'abstractive' here does not mean abstracting a universal from singulars, but quasi-imaginative cognition, which God can give without intuition. So the need for prior intuition or phantasms does not apply.
claims: Abstractive cognition in this sense is not abstraction of universals and need not presuppose intuition.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4229.summary: Replies to the eighth argument: imaginative cognition would reach the bare divine essence without becoming intuitive. On representation: it would be either a pure act conserved by God with no intermediate species, or by a species that determines formally rather than represents objectively, which is no more problematic than the view that God is seen in heaven through a species.
claims: Imaginative cognition can reach the bare divine essence without being intuitive.
A formally determining species would not prevent knowledge of God in himself.

ol96b1-bb5646-d1e4262.summary: Replies to the last argument: intellectual quasi-visual intuition is not material. 'Abstractive' is not a very apt term; better to say 'quasi-imaginative' and 'quasi-visual' or 'quasi-intuitive', since both words are carried over from sensory to intellectual cognition.
claims: Intellectual intuition is immaterial.
'Quasi-imaginative' is a better term than 'abstractive'.
